$\sim 55\,\%$ of the synthetic stripped stars in the SMC and $\sim 67\,\%$ in the LMC have reddening larger than the average reddening correction used by the 57 UV-excess survey. This suggests the uniform correction assumed in SUMS underestimates the effects of reddening for the majority of the observed population.

In both Clouds, we see a sharp drop-off in the detection rate for sources with $A_{V}\geq 0.5$ mag and no UV-excess detections for sources with $A_{V}\geq 1$ mag. In the SMC, $45\,\%$ of the stripped stars with intrinsic UV excess (corresponding to $\sim 14\,\%$ of the total population) have $A_{V}\geq 0.3$ mag, and are missing from the final UV-excess sample due to underestimated extinction. Similarly, our simulations predict that roughly $60\,\%$ of the intrinsic UV excess population (corresponding to $\sim 26\,\%$ of the total population) are missing from the final detected sample due to having $A_{V}\geq 0.45$ mag. There is no strong correlation between stripped star mass and reddening.

We find that a small number of simulated candidates with high extinction ( $A_{V}=0.5-1$ mag) are recovered via UV excess. The majority of these are stripped-star binaries with compact object companions. Due to their large intrinsic UV excess, the bluest of these sources can exhibit UV excess even in relatively dusty regions. A small minority of candidates with high extinction have MS companions. These sources typically have bad Tractor photometry due to being injected near a real source in the Swift-UVOT image. This can lead to overestimated UV flux by the Tractor, which can make the sources appear bluer than they are intrinsically. Most are flagged during the quality cuts, but a small fraction survive (see Section IV.2.2).

### IV.4 Mass distribution

Figure 15 shows the stripped star and companion mass distribution of the simulated population. We only show the companion masses for MS companions since we do not compute masses for compact object companions (Section III.1.4).

*Figure 15: Stripped star and companion mass distribution for the synthetic population in the SMC (left) and LMC (right). For the compact object companion systems, we only show the stripped star mass, since we do not model the properties of the companion in our binary synthesis (Section III.1.4). Grey markers show the entire synthetic population. Colored markers show sources that pass all candidate selection criteria. The UV-excess search is more sensitive to lower-mass stripped stars and companions. The typical stripped stars that pass all selection criteria are $M_{\rm stripped}\lesssim 5\,M_{\odot}$ and host low-mass MS companions ( $M_{\rm MS}\lesssim 5\,M_{\odot}$ ).*

We find that all detected stripped stars have relatively low-mass MS companions, with no stripped stars hosting $M_{\rm MS}\gtrsim 10\,M_{\odot}$ companions detected in either Cloud. Even among the most massive intermediate-mass stripped stars ( $M_{\rm{stripped}}\sim 7-8\,M_{\odot}$ ), only a few with MS companions are recovered in our forward model. Although massive stripped stars are intrinsically brighter, our results suggest that the detection efficiency of the search peaks at $M_{\rm stripped}\sim 2\,M_{\odot}$ . This likely reflects the correlation between stripped star and companion masses in our model. The results of our simulations are consistent with the predictions of 13, who predict (their Figure S8) that UV excess is typically detected for stripped-star binaries with $M_{\rm MS}<(1.4-2.5)M_{\rm stripped}$ .

The stripped-star mass is predicted to be correlated with its age. Thus, an upper bound on the detectable stripped-star mass allows us to constrain the age of the observed stripped stars. Stripped stars less massive than $\sim 5\,M_{\odot}$ are predicted to be at least $\sim 10$ Myr old since envelope stripping, while stripped stars less massive than $\sim 2\,M_{\odot}$ are predicted to be least $\sim 50$ Myr old [37]. This suggests that the majority of the observed stripped stars from SUMS are likley at least $(10-50)$ Myr old. We expect fewer stripped stars younger than $(5-10)$ Myr, because they are more likely to host massive companions, which dilute the UV excess of the stripped star.

### IV.5 Comparison to the SUMS candidates

Below, we compare our simulated population to the photometric stripped star candidates from SUMS [57].

#### IV.5.1 Spatial distribution

Figure 16 shows the spatial distribution of our forward-modeled population and the SUMS photometric candidates.

*Figure 16: Spatial distribution of the stripped-star candidates in the SMC (left) and LMC (right). The gray markers show all SUMS photometric candidates (both “Blue” and “Very Blue”), and the orange stars show the subset that has been spectroscopically confirmed [13]. The blue/pink markers show the mock observed stripped stars, with the darker colored markers representing the “Very Blue” systems. In both Clouds, we find that observed candidates are more clustered compared to the simulated sources, which are more uniformly distributed.*

We find that the synthetic population is more smoothly distributed than the observed candidates, which appear clustered.

The clusters in the observed population trace regions smaller than the grid sizes of the star formation history from Rubele et al. [85] and Mazzi et al. [60], which we use to forward model the simulated stripped star population (see Section III.2). The clusters are typically $(5-50)$ pc in diameter, while the subregions from the VMC survey have a diameter of $\sim 100$ pc. This suggests that these observed features may be smeared out in our simulated sample due to the spatial resolution of the star formation history.

Conversely, it is possible that these clusters are artificial features which are the results of spurious photometry within dense star clusters. These clustered regions contain a significantly larger fraction of faint UV sources ( $\gtrsim 19$ mag) than the rest of the observed candidate population. One explanation for the overdensity of faint candidates is poor background subtraction due to excess light from nebulae surrounding star clusters. Imperfect background modeling can result in an overestimation of UV fluxes and thus spurious UV excess. For example, NGC 371 in the SMC – which traces one of the largest clusters of the SUMS candidates – is surrounded by a large H II region that is easily visible in broadband optical images. The cluster is much younger [43, $5-10$ Myr; ] than the typical age ( $\sim 50$ Myr) of stripped stars we recover via UV excess (see Section IV.4). This is particularly true for the faint ( $\sim 19$ mag) sources, which would be low-mass stripped stars, which have longer life times ( $\gtrsim 50$ Myr). This suggests a large fraction of the photometric candidates in these young star clusters may be false positives. Higher-resolution UV photometry (e.g., from HST) may be able to distinguish between these scenarios.

#### IV.5.2 Predicted magnitude distribution

Figure 17 compares the distribution of UV magnitudes for our simulated sources and the observed stripped-star candidates.

*Figure 17: Magnitude distributions for each UV band measured by the Tractor. The shaded gray histogram shows the magnitude distribution of the SUMS candidates. The dashed black line shows the SUMS candidates with “Excellent” rankings (i.e., ‘VB-E’ and ‘B-E’). The solid blue/pink histogram shows the simulated candidates. The dashed blue/pink line shows all simulated stripped stars with mock observed photometry. The observed and simulated distributions agree in the intermediate magnitude range ( $\sim 16-18$ mag). In the intermediate magnitude range ( $16$ mag $\leq UV\leq 18$ mag), the forward-modeled population reproduces the observed SUMS distribution well. This suggests that the model predictions of the $(2-5)\,M_{\odot}$ stripped stars are consistent with observations. Most spectroscopically confirmed stripped stars from 13 also fall within this range. However, larger discrepancies between the observed candidates and simulated population are found at both brighter and fainter magnitudes.

For bright sources ( $UV\lesssim 16$ AB mag), we recover few to no candidates in the simulation, even though the underlying synthetic stripped star population (dashed lines in Figure 17) contains them. In our model, these bright sources are typically massive stripped stars ( $M_{\rm stripped}\gtrsim 6\,M_{\odot}$ ), which host relatively bright and massive companions, which dilute the UV excess of the stripped stars. This could imply that the brightest observed candidates are false positives. However, it is also possible that the masses of stripped stars and their companions are less strongly correlated in the observed sample compared to the synthetic population. This could occur, for example, if mass transfer is less conservative than assumed in our binary population synthesis model. We also caution that massive stripped stars, $M_{\rm stripped}\gtrsim 7\,M_{\odot}$ , are not as well modeled in our population because we determine their properties through extrapolation (see Section III.1).

At fainter magnitudes ( $UV\gtrsim 19$ mag, corresponding to stripped stars with masses of $M_{\rm stripped}\sim 1.5\,M_{\odot}$ formed from $M_{\rm init}\sim 6\,M_{\odot}$ ), the SUMS catalog contains $5-10$ times more stripped-star candidates compared to our simulations, and roughly twice the stripped stars compared to the underlying synthetic population. This suggests several things: (i) the model significantly underpredicts the number of faint stripped stars, or (ii) a fraction of the faint observed candidates are other types of stars and thus are false-positive candidates. It is possible that adjustments to the underlying population model could alleviate some of this discrepancy. For example, we could increase the initial binary fraction rate for stars with $M_{\rm init}\sim 6\,M_{\odot}$ , or use a non-uniform initial mass ratio distribution to increase the number of stripped stars with low-mass companions. However, we show below that the excess of faint sources is likely at least in part due to contamination by young MS stars.

### IV.6 Purity of the photometric catalog

The purity of the SUMS catalog is uncertain, and as discussed in 57, one of the main expected contaminants is luminous MS stars (with other potential contaminants, including AGB stars and rapidly-accreting WDs, also discussed in 57). All MS stars by definition lie redward of the ZAMS; however, if a source has less extinction than the average $A_{V}$ assumed or has blended photometry that overestimates its UV flux, it can lie blueward of the ZAMS and exhibit UV excess. Below, we forward model a population of MS stars to test the level of contamination.

We construct a synthetic MS population for the SMC, using isochrones from MIST [12, 8] with a metalicity of [Fe/H] = -1.00. We use the “Swift” synthetic photometry to model the Swift-UVOT photometry and the “UBVRIplus” synthetic photometry to model the MCPS photometry. We convert the UV photometry given in Vega magnitude to AB magnitudes using the conversions from Table 2. We assume an initial mass function from [49] and the star formation history from [85]. We limit our population to MS stars formed in the past 500 Myr, since we expect stars detected in the Swift images to be relatively young and massive. We assign a spatial coordinate and distance to each source using the same procedure described in Section III.2.4, and assign extinction by integrating the dust models described in Section III.3. We inspect the UV-optical CMDs and find that the blue edge of the MIST synthetic MS is significantly bluer than that of the observed MS in the SUMS catalog. To improve the agreement between the shape of the observed and simulated MSs, we apply empirical corrections to the predicted photometry: $UVW2=UVW2_{\rm MIST}+0.3$ , $UVM2=UVM2_{\rm MIST}+0.2$ , $UVW1=UVW1_{\rm MIST}+0.2$ , $V=V_{\rm MIST}-0.2$ , $I=I_{\rm MIST}-0.1$ , and $B=B_{\rm MIST}-0.25$ . These corrections make the simulated MS stars redder than predicted by MIST, reducing the number of contaminants. In Figure 18, we plot a UV-optical CMD of the synthetic MS population and compare it to the UV photometric catalog from 57.

*Figure 18: Left: UV-optical CMD with of Swift-UVOT sources from 57 (gray). In blue, we show the synthetic population of MS stars. The black dashed line shows the theoretical ZAMS and the gray dashed line shows the ZAMS offset by 0.4 indicating the “Blue” vs “Very Blue” cut off. Right: CMD of the 15,000 synthetic MS stars injected into Swift images. Blue markers show the 12 sources that pass all quality cuts and thus would contaminate the UV-excess selected sample of stripped stars. The contaminant MS stars have significantly overestimated UV fluxes, mainly due to crowding. Such sources are likely to appear as stripped-star candidates in UV-excess searches. Our simulations predict $\sim 120$ MS contaminates, but this predicted contamination rate is sensitive to the adopted photometric corrections.*

We randomly sample a subset of 15,000 stars from a population of $\sim$ 150,000 stars, which represent the total population of MS stars that lie inside the SUMS footprint and have $U<20.5$ mag. We inject these sources into the Swift-UVOT images and perform photometry using the Tractor as described in Section III.4.2. In the right panel of Figure 18, we show one of the UV-optical CMDs of the injected sample of 15,000 MS stars. We apply the photometric and SED quality cuts described in Section III.5 and require that sources exhibit UV excess in at least four of the nine UV-optical color combinations. Of the 15,000 MS stars, 12 pass all candidate selection criteria. Seven of the false-positive sources are classified as ‘B-G’ and another two as ‘B-E.’ Only three source have a ‘VB’ color. With a contamination rate of $0.08\%$ for $\sim 150,000$ MS stars, our forward model predicts $\sim 120$ contaminants in the SMC.

We find that most of the false-positive sources have UV magnitudes reported by the Tractor that are $>0.5$ mag brighter than the intrinsic brightness of the source. This is because the majority of these sources are injected into crowded regions and have a bright neighboring source within $3$ arcsec. Due to crowding, the Tractor is unable to disentangle the flux of the two sources, leading to an overestimated UV flux. All of the simulated false-positive sources make the final UV-excess detection because of their overestimated UV fluxes, not because they fall in regions of low reddening. Figure 19 shows the distribution of flux fractions for the observed candidates, simulated stripped stars, and simulated MS stars. A majority of the MS contaminants have relatively low flux fractions, reflecting the fact that they are located in crowded regions and have overestimated UV fluxes.

This possibility was recognized by 57. This motivated their flux fraction cut, in which all sources with flux fractions below 0.1 were removed, as well as those with flux fractions below 0.25 that have a neighboring source within $2.5^{\prime\prime}$ . This criteria was designed to strike a balance between eliminating contaminants (i.e. the strong overdensity of SUMS candidates with low flux fraction in Figure 19; also see Figure 19 in Appendix of 57) while also keeping sources for future follow-up. While fewer than $10\,\%$ of the simulated stripped stars have flux fractions below 0.5, $\sim 65\,\%$ of SUMS candidates have flux fractions below 0.5. Our simulations show that the excess of SUMS candidates with low flux fractions may be explained by false-positive candidates.

The number of predicted contaminants in the SMC ( $\sim 120$ ) is roughly half the number of photometric stripped-star candidates from SUMS (298). This contamination rate is somewhat higher than the $\sim 15\,\%$ found in the 13 spectroscopic sample. However, as discussed in Section II, the preliminary version of the survey by 13 used a different selection function, including manual selection of photometric candidates, which prioritized brighter sources with cleaner photometry than most of the photometric candidates. We find the inferred false-positive rate is sensitive to the photometric offsets that we apply to the MIST photometry, because the main selection of the UV-excess search relies on color measurements. When the photometric corrections are varied, the false-positive rate can vary significantly. For example, repeating the simulations without any photometric offsets, we estimate $\sim 2,400$ false positives in the SMC (which is significantly larger than the total number of photometric candidates that were found by SUMS). Thus, it is difficult to precisely predict the number of false positives in the SUMS catalog. However, the above experiment suggests that we can expect up to a few hundred false positives due to MS stars, and faint candidates ( $>18.5$ mag) with low flux fractions ( $<0.5$ ) are the most likely to be contaminants.

## V Summary and Discussion

Recently, the first sample of intermediate-mass stripped stars in the MCs was discovered via a UV-excess survey (Figure 1). This effort produced the SUMS catalog, which contains 820 photometric candidates [57]. Of these, 16 have been confirmed spectroscopically [13]. Our population synthesis model predicts that $\sim 1/3$ of stripped-star binaries show UV excess intrinsically. However, UV-excess searches for stripped stars are affected by several selection effects which decrease the survey completeness: (i) dust extinction and (ii) bright companions, which reduce the UV excess of stripped stars, and (iii) crowding and (iv) Swift survey coverage, which limit the completeness of the UV photometry. In this work, we forward model a synthetic population of stripped stars to characterize the selection function of SUMS and constrain properties of the full population. Our main results are as follows:

- (i) Stripped star population synthesis: we create a synthetic population of intermediate-mass ( $1-10\,M_{\odot}$ ) stripped stars in the MCs. By combining binary population synthesis with spatially-resolved star formation histories (Figures 2 and 4), we estimate the number, mass, and age distribution of stripped stars in each Cloud. Our model predicts $\sim 1,000$ stripped stars in the SMC and $\sim 2,500$ in the LMC (Section III.2.1), which are comparable to predictions from other studies [37, e.g., ]. We spatially distribute simulated stripped stars so that their small-scale clustering follows that of young MS stars in the Clouds (Figure 4). We assume an exponential dust density distribution along the line of sight that is constrained by observations of the total integrated extinction column at each spatial location. This results in a realistic distribution of dust extinction, including both contributions internal to the Clouds and foreground extinction from the MW.

- (ii) UV mock photometry: we inject each synthetic stripped star into the Swift-UVOT images used by SUMS and perform mock photometry using the photometric pipeline from 57 (Figure 7). By doing the injection and recovery, this allows us to model the selection biases from the finite spatial coverage of the Swift-UVOT survey and blending of a stripped star’s light with nearby sources in crowded regions. Using this pipeline, we recover $\sim 54\,\%$ (SMC) and $\sim 36\,\%$ (LMC) of our injected sources. We fail to recover photometry for the remaining sources because they are either: (a) located outside of the SUMaC footprint, (b) located in one of the masked regions near a bright source, or (c) removed in post-processing of the Tractor outputs. We reject sources with bad photometry based on the selection criteria described in 57. Our finding suggests that $\sim 10\,\%$ of stripped stars with robust intrinsic UV excess are missing from the final stripped-star catalog due to lack of good photometry alone.

- (iii) UV-excess selection: we apply the full SUMS selection criteria, including photometric and SED quality cuts, and UV-excess selection, to our simulated population (Figure 8). We find a stripped-star recovery rate of $(10.9\,\pm\,0.5)\,\%$ for the SMC and $(7.0\,\pm\,0.2)\,\%$ for the LMC (Figure 10). Of the sources that show intrinsic UV excess, $(31.3\,\pm\,4.3)\,\%$ and $(15.3\,\pm\,0.6)\,\%$ of the simulated stripped-star systems are recovered; correcting for the SUMS footprint, this corresponds to a detection rate of $\sim 47\,\%$ (SMC) and $\sim 33\,\%$ (LMC) for the intrinsic UV-excess sources. The lower recovery rate in the LMC is likely a result of a combination of factors, including higher reddening due to dust and more crowding. Further, we classify our sources into four categories following 57 (Table 3). Most of the synthetic stripped stars are classified as “Excellent” candidates, with similar numbers of sources classified as “Blue” and “Very Blue.”

- (iv) Completeness of the photometric catalog: we predict that over $90\,\%$ of the intermediate-mass stripped stars in the MCs are not recovered by the UV-excess survey conducted by 57. The recovered stripped star population misses sources that: (a) host massive ( $M_{\rm MS}\geq 5-7\,M_{\odot}$ ) MS companions (Figure 11, 15), (b) lie in regions of high star density, or (c) have extinction of $A_{V}\geq(0.5-1)$ mag (Figure 13, 14). The simulations predict that such sources will not be selected by SUMS, even under ideal conditions. Stripped stars with compact object companions are more sensitive to the UV-excess survey since the companion does not dilute the stripped stars’ UV excess. As a result, they are overrepresented in the detected population. While only $\sim 10\,\%$ of intrinsic stripped stars host compact object companions in the model, we find that they make up about $22\,\%$ of the detected candidates. The overall recovery rate could be improved by carrying out surveys with higher spatial resolution or modeling extinction on a source-by-source basis (see Section V.2).

- (v) Purity of the photometric catalog: we compare the spatial distribution (Figure 16) and UV magnitudes (Figure 17) of the SUMS photometric candidates to our simulated population. In the observed sample, we find an excess of spatially clustered, faint photometric candidates ( $UV\sim 19$ mag, which correspond to stripped stars of mass $M_{\rm stripped}\lesssim 1.5\,M_{\odot}$ ), that are not present in the synthetic population. We suspect that many of these sources are false positives due to (a) bad photometry in crowded regions, or (b) contamination by other types of UV-bright sources like young MS stars. We forward model a population of MS stars using the same methods we used for stripped stars to test for false positives (Figure 18). Most contaminants will likely have small UV flux fractions ( $<0.5$ ), faint magnitudes ( $>18.5$ mag), and moderate UV excess (Figure 19). This implies higher contamination rates for faint candidates in crowded regions, which are typically classified as “Blue” candidates. The “flux_frac” (the flux fraction) and “dist_neighbor” (distance to the nearest neighbor) computed for the SUMS candidates in 57 can be used to identify sources that have a higher likelihood of being contaminants and thus warrant greater caution.

- (vi) Implications for stripped-star population synthesis and binary evolution: We find that the binary synthesis models used in this paper [28] the observed intermediate-mass systems ( $M_{\rm stripped}=2-5\,M_{\odot}$ ) reasonably well but fail to match the higher-mass ( $\gtrsim 5\,M_{\odot}$ ) and lower-mass ( $\lesssim 2\,M_{\odot}$ ) ends of the observed population (Section IV.5.2). This suggests that the assumptions adopted in our population models (Section III.1) which we take as ground truth– such as the treatment of mass transfer, overshooting, and CEE– are broadly consistent with the observed population, at least in the intermediate-mass regime. The underprediction of high- and low-mass systems may be indicative of problems in the model but could also be a result of contamination of the observed candidates. Large-scale spectroscopic follow-up of the SUMS photometric candidates is necessary to distinguish between these possibilities.

### V.1 Dependence of UV-excess detection rate on the underlying population

The recovery rate of stripped stars is sensitive to the assumptions made in modeling the underlying population. In our simulations, we take the binary population synthesis models described in Section III.1 as ground truth. Below, we discuss how these assumptions affect the synthetic stripped star population and its detectability in UV-excess surveys.

Mass transfer efficiency is one of the most important factors in determining the detectability of stripped-star binaries via UV excess. However, it remains uncertain observationally, with a range of sometimes contradictory constraints presented in literature [75, 96, 95, 6, 55, e.g., ]. Adjusting the mass transfer efficiency in our binary population synthesis models would alter the properties of the simulated stripped star population and could lead to different detection rates in a UV-excess survey. For example, a higher mass transfer efficiency is likely to result in brighter and more massive MS companions to stripped stars. Given our finding that a UV-excess search is most sensitive to lower-mass companions, a binary population produced with a higher mass transfer efficiency would likely produce a population which will have a lower detection rate.

The overshoot parameter is another important factor in stellar evolution models that strongly influences the predicted properties of simulated stripped-star populations. For example, population synthesis models that adopt a smaller overshooting parameter than the one we use predict significantly few stripped stars [104, e.g., ]. We expect both the number and brightness of stripped stars to be correlated with this parameter, and therefore predict that the detection rate will likely be sensitive to this value.

The initial binary population assumed in our stripped-star population synthesis is expected to affect the final predicted population. For example, a more bottom-heavy initial mass function or a higher binary fraction for low-mass primaries, could help alleviate some of the discrepancies between the observed population from SUMS and the synthetic population. We also assume that $7\,\%$ of stripped stars have compact object companions. Increasing this fraction would result in a higher detection rate of stripped-star binaries.

We also note that our underlying population does not account for single stripped stars, which are predicted theoretically [78, 107, 80, e.g., ]. Observational evidence exists for single sdO/B stars [22, 21, e.g., ] and such objects can be formed if a WD companion to a stripped star explodes as a Type Ia supernovae [42, e.g., ]. We do not include single stripped stars in our synthetic population, since they are likely rare, but we note that they could be overrepresented in observed samples selected by UV excess.

Further work is needed to quantify the sensitivity of our predictions on detectability of stripped stars via a UV-excess survey. Empirical measurements of the SUMS detection rate will allow us to directly compare the predictions from various population models to the observed rates. Combining these results with constraints from sdB and WR star binaries, we can also test the mass dependence of binary interaction processes for systems formed through similar formation channels. Improved spectral model grids are necessary for further development of stripped star binary population synthesis models and work is currently in progress to address this. We plan to further investigate the sensitivity of our results to the underlying binary population synthesis in future work.

### V.2 Uncovering the missing population of stripped stars

Several improvements could be made to UV-excess searches to increase their completeness.

Modeling extinction for individual sources via SED fitting, rather than assuming an average value for all sources, could increase the population detectable via UV excess. Our forward model predicts that about half the sources with robust intrinsic UV excess may be missed due to extinction. Precise measurements of reddening for individual sources might also allow for an extension of a similar survey to the MW, where reddening is more severe but 3D dust maps exist.

Conducting a similar search using UV data from surveys with higher resolution or deeper photometry would allow us to significantly increase the number of stripped stars detectable via UV excess. Current missions such as the Ultra Violet Imaging Telescope [51, UVIT; ], and future missions like the Ultraviolet Explorer [50, UVEX; ], are promising for follow-up studies and deeper explorations. These surveys also cover the FUV, which reaches shorter wavelengths than any of the Swift-UVOT bands, making them well-suited for studying UV-bright sources.

Lastly, to uncover stripped-star binaries with massive companions, a different search method, such as a spectroscopic search using surveys like SDSS-V [48] or light curve modeling [64, e.g.] will be required.

## Appendix A Estimating the dust disk scale height and inclination

For each Cloud, we choose a small patch of the sky with significant extinction. Following Section IV.6, we model a synthetic population of MS stars for the small patch. We then apply extinction to each of the synthetic MS stars based on the extinction model we describe in Section III.3. We vary the dust scale height $h_{d}$ , and compare each of the resulting synthetic CMDs against the observed MCPS population from the same region of the sky. By comparing the observed spread and shape of the MS to the synthetic population, we estimate a dust scale height for each of the Clouds.

For the SMC, we restrict our analysis to $(11.8\rm{\ deg}<\rm{RA}<12.2\rm{\ deg})$ and $(-73.3\rm{\ deg}<\rm{Dec}<-73.05\rm{\ deg})$ . The top panels of Figure 20 show some examples of the synthetic CMD with $h_{\rm d}=0.01,0.1,0.3,0.5$ kpc. We find that the synthetic and observed MS best agrees for $h_{d}\sim 0.3$ kcp. Since the geometry of the SMC is not well constrained we also repeat the analysis by applying an tilt to the disk (i.e., an inclination $i$ ), while fixing the scale height to $h_{\rm d}=0.3$ . We compare the synthetic and observed CMDs for $i=$ -30, -50, 0, 30, 50 degrees. We find that since we take the total integrated extinction at $z=\infty$ to be fixed, there is little to no correlation between inclination and the extinction map. Thus, we assume no inclination for the SMC.

## Abstract

We present discovery of SMASH J004005 $-$ 733351, an intermediate-mass stripped helium star in the Small Magellanic Cloud with a dark companion. The system was identified in a new optical color-selected survey for stripped stars and confirmed through spectroscopic follow-up. We measure an orbital period of $P_{\rm orb}=19.95\pm 0.002$ hours and a radial-velocity semi-amplitude of $K=91.7^{+3.2}_{-3.1}\,{\rm km\,s^{-1}}$ . Simultaneous modeling of the optical spectrum and ultraviolet-to-optical spectral energy distribution yields a stripped star evolutionary mass $M_{\rm stripped}=3.84\pm 0.54\,M_{\odot}$ , temperature $T_{\rm eff}=68.3\pm 6.4$ kK, surface gravity $\log g=4.76\pm 0.12$ , luminosity $\log(L/L_{\odot})=4.28\pm 0.13$ , radius $R=0.99\pm 0.09\,R_{\odot}$ , and an unusually high surface hydrogen abundance of $X_{\rm H,s}=0.63\pm 0.04$ . The companion is undetected spectroscopically, and the orbital solution and stripped-star evolutionary mass imply a minimum companion mass of $M_{2}\gtrsim 1.2\,M_{\odot}$ . The absence of photometric variability from irradiation rules out a main-sequence companion. The companion is most likely a neutron star (NS), although a massive white dwarf or low-mass stripped star cannot be fully excluded. Binary evolution models predict that the stripped star will refill its Roche lobe after core helium exhaustion, likely producing a stripped or ultra-stripped supernova and ultimately a double NS binary if the system survives. SMASH J004005 $-$ 733351 is among the first known stripped stars with a compact object companion. The system provides a new empirical benchmark for the late stages of binary interaction that lead to (ultra-)stripped supernovae and double NS binaries.

## I Introduction

A star can lose its hydrogen envelope through binary interaction or stellar winds, leaving behind a stripped helium star. Binary evolution models predict envelope stripping for a wide range of stellar masses. Low-mass ( $\lesssim 1\,M_{\odot}$ ) stripped stars are commonly referred to as hot subdwarf (sdB/O) stars [45, 46] and are formed via binary interactions [43, 42], such as stable mass transfer or common-envelope evolution (CEE). Massive stripped stars ( $\gtrsim 8\,M_{\odot}$ ) can appear as Wolf-Rayet (WR) stars [12, 105]. WR stars can be formed either by binary interactions, or by wind-driven mass loss, which is likely most important for the most massive stars. In contrast to their low- and high-mass counterparts, intermediate-mass stripped stars, though predicted for decades [60, e.g.,], have only recently been observationally confirmed [17, 37, 72, 80, 69]; and the confirmed population remains small.

The majority of stripped stars formed via binary interactions are predicted to host main-sequence (MS) companions [35, 131, e.g.,]. After the initially more massive star undergoes envelope stripping and core helium ignition, the less massive companion, which has a longer evolutionary timescale, remains on the MS. In some cases, after the stripped star has evolved into a compact object– a white dwarf (WD), neutron star (NS), or black hole (BH), depending on its mass– the system can undergo a second phase of binary interaction. This stage strips the originally less massive star, producing a stripped star with a compact object companion [110, 36, e.g., ]. Such systems are particularly interesting because they represent the outcome of two distinct stages of stripping and are predicted to be direct progenitors of (ultra-) stripped-envelope supernovae [108, 18, 21, 74, e.g., ] and double compact-object binaries [114, e.g.,].

However, intermediate-mass stripped stars with compact-object companions remain observationally elusive. PSR J1928+1815 was recently proposed to have an intermediate-mass helium stripped star [129], but deep near-infrared imaging ruled out the stripped-star companion [81]. A subset of the confirmed intermediate-mass stripped stars in the MCs identified by [17] exhibit SB1-type spectra, with no evidence of a luminous companion. [69] confirmed the binary nature of several of these systems, but the nature of their companions remains uncertain. An additional system from the sample of [17], not included in the analysis of [69], was reported by Ludwig [73] to host a compact-object companion. A full analysis of that system will be presented in Ludwig et al. (in preparation).

Confirming compact companions to intermediate-mass stripped stars is important for testing binary evolution models and constraining the formation channels of ultra-stripped supernovae (SNe) and gravitational-wave sources. Currently, there are no empirical constraints on the fraction of binaries that survive the second stripping phase [127, 36, e.g.,], and observations of such systems are needed to constrain these models.

In this paper, we present a newly discovered intermediate-mass stripped star in a binary with a dark companion: SMASH J004005-733351 (hereafter J0040-7333). We identified J0040-7333 in the Small Magellanic Cloud (SMC) as part of a survey for intermediate-mass stripped stars using an optical blue-excess selection. We conduct spectroscopic and photometric analysis of this system and find that: (i) the system is in a relatively compact orbit with a period of $\sim 20$ hours; (ii) its spectra and broadband spectral energy distribution (SED) are dominated by an intermediate-mass stripped star; (iii) the binary mass function implies a minimum companion mass of $M_{\rm comp}\gtrsim 1.2\,{\rm M_{\odot}}$ ; (iv) light curve modeling rules out a low-mass MS companion, implying instead a compact-object or stripped-star companion; and (v) evolutionary models favor a NS.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. In Section II, we discuss the optical search for stripped stars and the discovery of J0040-7333. In Section III, we outline the data used for the analysis of the system, including optical and ultraviolet (UV) photometry, optical spectra, and an optical light curve. In Section IV, we describe our analysis methods and present our results, including the orbital solution and the physical properties of the stripped star and its companion. In Section V, we discuss possible formation channels and future evolution, and discuss the nature of the companion. In Section VI, we compare the newly discovered system to related populations. Finally, we summarize our results in Section VII.

## II Discovery

During their long-lived core-helium-burning phase, most stripped stars are predicted to be hot and compact, making them UV-bright compared to MS stars of similar luminosity [33, 34]. Motivated by this prediction, [17] carried out a UV-excess survey in the Magellanic Clouds (MCs) to search for intermediate-mass stripped stars. Their search yielded 16 spectroscopically-confirmed stripped stars (4 in the SMC and 12 in the LMC). However, population synthesis models predict that many hundreds more intermediate-mass stripped stars should exist in the MCs [130, 51, e.g.,], indicating that the initial survey likely only discovered the tip of the iceberg.

A complete list of photometric candidates identified using the general method described in [17] was published in [72]. This revealed an additional 820 photometric candidates. This sample of candidates, however, remains limited by the spatial resolution and coverage [4] of the Swift Ultraviolet Survey of the Magellanic Clouds [41, SUMaC;]. To identify stripped star candidates inaccessible to the [72] search, we carried out a complementary search using optical photometry.

We found that the spectroscopically-confirmed stripped stars from [17] exhibit blue excess in the optical $u$ -band data from the Survey of the Magellanic Stellar History [84, SMASH; ], suggesting that similar stripped stars can potentially be selected based on optical photometry alone. We show this in a color-magnitude diagram (CMD) in Figure 1. Motivated by this, we conducted an optical blue-excess survey using SMASH photometry. The UV-excess search of [17] and [72] used UV photometry from the SUMaC, obtained with the Swift Ultraviolet/Optical Telescope [101, UVOT;], and optical photometry from the Magellanic Cloud Photometric Survey [132, MCPS;]. Although restricting the search to optical wavelengths limits our sensitivity to only the most extreme UV-excess systems, the SMASH survey has two advantages: (i) larger footprint, and (ii) higher spatial resolution, with PSF FWHM of $\sim 1^{\prime\prime}$ compared to the $\sim 2.4^{\prime\prime}$ PSF of Swift-UVOT. This allows us to search for intermediate-mass stripped stars in regions previously unexplored and probe crowded fields where the existing UV photometry is affected by blending. In particular, the newly discovered stripped star we present in this paper (J0040-7333) was not identified in previous UV-excess surveys of the Magellanic Clouds [17, 72] because it lies outside the SUMaC footprint.

### II.1 Candidate selection

We carried out a search for intermediate-mass stripped stars in the SMC. We identified candidates in SMASH with $(u-g)$ colors and $g$ -band magnitude similar to known intermediate-mass stripped stars. We applied a series of quality cuts to this population and selected 27 of the most promising candidates for spectroscopic follow-up (see Figure 1):

- • We required the candidate to have $(u-g)$ color and $g$ -band magnitudes (AB) consistent with the spectroscopically confirmed intermediate-mass stripped stars: $15<g<18.9$ , $14(u-g)+15.5<g<14(u-g)+21$ . We checked all point sources in the SMASH catalog with $9<{\rm RA\,(deg)}<24$ and $-74<{\rm Dec\,(deg)}<-70$ and identified 441 candidates.

- • Further, we rejected candidates with Gaia [28, 29] parallaxes and proper motions inconsistent with SMC membership. We required parallax_over_error (i.e., the measured parallax of a source divided by its uncertainty) to be $<3$ . For SMC sources, we expect this quantity to be small, because at SMC distances the true parallax ( $\approx 0.02$ mas) is smaller than the Gaia parallax uncertainties for faint sources. We also required proper motions within $2\sigma$ of the bulk motion of the SMC [134]. After rejecting possible foreground and background sources, we were left with 238 candidates.

- • Finally, we selected sources with the highest-quality SMASH photometry. We required each source to pass two SMASH quality flags: chi $<3$ and $-1<$ sharp $<1$ . These parameters are outputs of the DAOPHOT PSF-fitting routine reported in the SMASH catalog. The chi parameter measures the scatter in the PSF-fit residuals. The sharp parameter measures the relative width of the best-fit PSF profile compared to the expected stellar PSF. This rejects an additional 151 candidates. We visually inspected the $g$ - and $u$ -band SMASH images of the remaining candidates and rejected sources with potentially contaminated photometry due to crowding. We selected 27 candidates with the best photometry.

### II.2 Spectroscopic follow-up and confirmation

Most core helium burning stripped stars are predicted to be significantly hotter than typical MS stars of similar luminosity with effective temperatures reaching $T_{\rm eff}\gtrsim 40-100\,{\rm kK}$ [34]. As a result, they are expected to show strong He ii absorption lines (e.g., He ii $\lambda\lambda 4200,4542,4686,5412$ ) which are not expected for MS stars of similar luminosity. These unique spectral features allow systems that contain stripped stars to be identified with a single epoch of spectroscopy, if their photometry is dominated by the stripped star. We note that intermediate-mass stripped stars usually do not show He ii emission, unlike their higher-mass counterparts (i.e., WR stars) because they are not sufficiently luminous to drive strong winds that produce detectable wind lines in the optical. This is especially true in low-metallicity environments, such as the SMC [123, 37, e.g.,]. However, see Müller-Horn et al. 80 for a recently discovered Galactic stripped star that shows emission in He ii.

We conducted spectroscopic follow-up of the 27 candidates using the Magellan Echellette (MagE; Marshall et al. 78) spectrograph. Of these, three appear to have spectra consistent with spectral models of intermediate-mass stripped stars. One source has optical spectra dominated by the stripped star component (J0040-7333), while the other two exhibit composite spectra containing features of both a stripped star and a luminous companion, similar to the ‘Class 2’ systems presented in [17]. In this paper, we focus on J0040-7333. A full description of the survey and analysis of the other stripped stars will be presented in future work.

#### III.1.1 Survey of the Magellanic Stellar History (SMASH)

The Survey of the Magellanic Stellar History (SMASH; Nidever et al. 84) imaged the MCs using the Dark Energy Camera (DECam; Flaugher et al. 26). The catalog provides optical photometry in $ugriz$ bands down to $\sim 24$ mag.

#### III.1.2 Magellanic Cloud Photometry Survey (MCPS)

The Magellanic Cloud Photometric Survey (MCPS; Zaritsky et al. 132) was conducted using the Great Circle Camera [133] on the $1\,{\rm m}$ Swope telescope at Las Campanas Observatory. The catalog provides photometry in $UBVI$ bands down to $U\sim 21.5$ , $B\sim 23.5$ , $V\sim 23$ and $I\sim 22$ mag.

#### III.1.3 Swift-Ultraviolet/Optical Telescope (UVOT)

The Ultraviolet/Optical Telescope (UVOT) is a UV/optical instrument onboard the Swift satellite [30, 101, 91, UVOT; ]. We identify 45 archival Swift-UVOT $UVW1$ -band observations of SMC fields containing J0040-7333. Of these, six images have problems with their WCS solutions. We performed PSF photometry on the remaining images using the photometric pipeline developed by [72], which uses The Tractor [67].

#### III.1.4 Ultraviolet Imaging Telescope (UVIT)

The Ultraviolet Imaging Telescope (UVIT; Kumar et al. 63) is a UV imager on the Astrosat satellite [107]. Several surveys of the SMC have been carried out [49, 50, e.g., ]. We downloaded the level-2 image named ‘‘SMC-2’’ from the Astrosat-UVIT archive11 1 https://astrobrowse.issdc.gov.in/astro_archive/archive/Home.jsp, and performed PSF-photometry using The Tractor. We follow the photometric pipeline developed for the Swift-UVOT images by [72] with several modifications. Because no theoretical PSF model is available for UVIT, we build our own empirical PSF model by taking bright and isolated stars from the “SMC-2” image and stacking their cutouts using the EPSFBuilder routine in photutils. We also modify the background subtraction to be less aggressive by relaxing the sigma-clipping criteria, since a large fraction of pixels in the UVIT image have zero or near-zero counts. We also relax the position prior to account for the asymmetric shape of the empirical UVIT PSF. Finally, we convert the measured detector count rates to magnitudes using the zero points for the appropriate UVIT filter [109]:

$$ m=-2.5\log_{10}(C)+16.274, $$

where $C$ is the count rate given in counts per second measured by The Tractor.

#### III.1.5 Optical Gravitational Lensing Experiment (OGLE)

The Optical Gravitational Lensing Experiment (OGLE; Udalski et al. 118, Udalski et al. 117, Udalski et al. 119) is a long-running optical time-domain survey conducted with the 1.3 m Warsaw Telescope at Las Campanas Observatory. We obtained a long-baseline OGLE light curve for J0040-7333. The $I-$ band light curve consists of 3860 epochs taken between 2001 and 2025. The median photometric uncertainty is 0.03 mag per observation.

### III.2 Spectroscopy

We obtained 16 spectra across 10 nights using two different instruments22 2 All reduced spectra are available here: https://www.dropbox.com/scl/fo/b0z3nrefb316onwau0x88/AMEQz8rWV1KeCLMnY6tFEyY?rlkey=4ekj5cehr1romddaorcb4flra&st=zy0n2r99&dl=0 (to be moved to Zenodo when the paper is accepted).: 12 epochs with the Magellan Echellette Spectrograph [78, MagE; ] on the Magellan Baade Telescope at Las Campanas Observatory, and 4 epochs with the Gemini Multi-Object Spectrograph (GMOS-S; Hook et al. 47) on the 8.1 m Gemini South Telescope at the Gemini South observatory. All observations are summarized in Table 4 in Appendix B; Figure 14 shows all follow-up spectra. Below, we describe the instrumental setups and data reduction methods used for the follow-up observations.

#### III.2.1 Magellan Echellette Spectrograph (MagE)

We used the 0.7 and 0.85 arcsec slits with $1\times 1$ binning for all MagE observations, with exposure times of $600-1800\,\rm{s}$ depending on observing conditions. The resulting spectra have resolution $R\sim 4100$ over a wavelength range of $\lambda\sim 3500-7000\,\rm{\AA}$ . For each science frame, we subsequently obtained an arc exposure after each observation, which was used by the reduction pipeline for wavelength calibrations. We reduce the data using PypeIt [93, 94]. We normalize each spectrum by fitting a polynomial to each echelle order. We reject $2\sigma$ outliers during the fit to mask absorption lines. We repeat this process iteratively until we obtain a stable normalized spectrum in each order. After clipping the low-sensitivity edges, we combine the orders by interpolating them onto a common wavelength grid and averaging the overlapping regions, weighting each pixel by the inverse variance.

#### III.2.2 Gemini Multi-Object Spectrographs (GMOS-S)

We used the B480 grating on GMOS-S with a central wavelength of 470 nm. Using the $0.75^{\prime\prime}$ slit and $1\times 1$ binning with 1200 s exposures, we obtain spectra with resolution of $R\sim 900$ for a wavelength range of $\lambda\sim 380-600$ nm. Each science observation is supplemented with an arc exposure, which is used for wavelength calibrations. We reduce the data using the standard configuration of the DRAGONS pipeline [64, 106] and normalize them using the polynomial-fitting method described in Section III.2.1. The GMOS-S spectra contain gaps in wavelength coverage due to space between CCD detectors. We choose a central wavelength such that most of the spectral features of interest fall within the regions covered by the detectors.

## IV Analysis

### IV.1 Constraining the orbit

We measure radial velocities (RVs) using the 16 epochs of follow-up spectra. We fit the resulting RVs with a Keplerian orbit.

#### IV.1.1 RV measurements

We measure RVs for each of the 16 spectra by cross-correlating the He ii and Balmer absorption lines with a stripped-star spectral model [39]. We perform the $\chi^{2}$ -fit using the model with $T_{\rm eff}=70$ kK, $\log(g/[\rm{cms}^{-2}])=5.0$ , and $X\rm{H}_{\rm s}=0.6$ , which provides a reasonable match to the observed spectra (we carry out a spectral fit in Section IV.2). After convolving the model to match the instrument resolution ( $R=4100$ for MagE and $R=900$ for GMOS-S), we generate a grid of Doppler-shifted spectra with RVs ranging from 40 to 350 km/s. We select 40 $\rm{\AA}$ -wide windows centered on several diagnostic lines (He ii $\lambda\lambda 4542,4686,5411$ and He ii/Balmer blends at He ii $\lambda 4100$ /H $\delta$ , He ii $\lambda 4339$ /H $\gamma$ , and He ii $\lambda 4860$ /H $\beta$ ) and compute the $\chi^{2}$ value for each RV. We visually inspect each line and exclude any problematic lines (e.g., lines affected by problematic background subtraction or located near defective detector pixels that mask a significant portion of the line profile.)

During the initial fitting stages, we tested different combinations and numbers of spectral lines. We restricted our fitting to $4000\,\rm{\AA}\lesssim\lambda\lesssim 5500\,\rm{\AA}$ because this wavelength range has the highest SNR and contains the most prominent optical features of stripped stars. Although the measured RVs vary somewhat across lines, the RVs measured from different lines are generally consistent within their uncertainties for well-sampled and unproblematic lines; see Appendix B for a comparison of RVs measured from pure He ii lines and He ii/Balmer blends. We found that the visual inspection step is necessary to exclude lines where the substantial portion of the line profile is affected by artifacts, preventing a reliable fit and RV measurement.

We sum the $\chi^{2}$ contributions from all lines to compute the total $\chi^{2}$ , $\chi_{\rm tot}^{2}$ , for each spectrum, and adopt the velocity corresponding to the minimum $\chi^{2}_{\rm tot}$ as the best-fit RV. At this stage, we also account for barycentric corrections. We show some example fits in Figure 2.

We estimate the uncertainties by identifying the range of RVs consistent with the best-fit value at the $1\sigma$ confidence level and round to the nearest integer. We include a $\pm 3\,{\rm km/s}$ systematic uncertainty, added in quadrature with the statistical uncertainty from the $\chi^{2}$ minimization, to account for potential biases introduced by fixing the spectral model. We report all RV measurements, observation times, and the set of lines used in the fitting procedure, in Table 4 in Appendix B.

#### IV.1.2 Constraining the orbital solution

We use the joker [92, v.1.3.1;], a rejection sampling code designed for binary RV data, coupled with a standard Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) method to constrain the orbital solution for J0040-7333. We fit for the six free parameters of a Keplerian RV orbit: orbital period ( $P_{\rm orb}$ ), RV semi-amplitude ( $K$ ), systemic velocity ( $v_{0}$ ), eccentricity ( $e$ ), argument of periastron ( $\omega$ ), and a phase parameter ( $\Delta t$ ). Here, $\Delta t=t_{0}-t_{\rm obs,min}$ , where $t_{\rm obs,min}$ (BJD = 2460849.808) is the time of the first observation and $t_{0}$ is the periastron time.

For the orbital period, we use a Jeffreys prior [55], $p(P_{\rm orb})\propto\frac{1}{P_{\rm orb}}$ , with a range of $0.5-5$ days. We select this range after an initial coarse sampling with orbital periods ranging from 1 hour up to 100 days, which showed that the RVs are only consistent with short orbital periods ( $\lesssim 5,{\rm days}$ ). For the RV semi-amplitude, we use a Gaussian prior with $\sigma_{K}=50$ km s-1 centered around $K=0$ . For the systemic velocity, we adopt a Gaussian prior with $\mu_{v_{0}}=160$ km s-1 and $\sigma_{v_{0}}=20$ km s-1, consistent with the bulk motion of the SMC. For the eccentricity, we assume a uniform prior between 0 and 1. We adopt uniform priors for all phase terms.

We first draw $N=50,000,000$ prior samples using the joker and retain them with probability proportional to their likelihood. This results in a single posterior mode with $P_{\rm orb}\approx 20$ hrs, indicating that no other orbital period provides a comparably good orbital solution to the observed RVs. We sample from the posterior using emcee [27] with 50 walkers, each taking 5,000 steps after a burn-in of 100 steps. We report both the median and maximum a posteriori (MAP) constraints in Table 2.

### IV.2 Constraining the properties of the stripped star

We simultaneously fit the normalized stacked spectrum (Section IV.2.2) and broadband SED to constrain the properties of the stripped star. We treat J0040-7333 as an SB1 system and assume that the optical and UV flux is dominated by the stripped star, with negligible contribution from the companion.

#### IV.2.1 Evolutionary models, synthetic spectra, and synthetic photometry

Evolutionary models: we use the evolutionary models for intermediate-mass stripped stars at SMC metallicity (Z = 0.002) presented in [34]. These models were computed using the Modules for Experiments in Stellar Astrophysics [85, 86, 87, 88, 89, 56, MESA; ]. The tracks assume Case B mass transfer, which is expected to be the most common channel for producing stripped stars [102], though theoretical models predict that stripped stars can also result from Case C mass transfer [23, e.g., ]. We define the stripped-star lifetime as the core-helium-burning phase, corresponding to $X_{\rm He,c}=0.001-0.95$ . The binary physics assumed in these models produce stripped stars with surface hydrogen abundances of $X_{\rm H,s}\approx 0.35-0.4$ . We interpolate between tracks with initial masses of $M_{i}=9.00-16.44\,{\rm M_{\odot}}$ to construct continuous evolutionary tracks, including relevant stellar properties (e.g., $T_{\rm eff}$ , $L$ , $M_{\rm stripped}$ ) as a function of evolutionary phase.

Spectral models: we interpolate a grid of spectral models of intermediate-mass stripped stars [39] to produce synthetic spectra for any given combination of $T_{\rm eff}$ , $\log(g)$ , and $X_{\rm H,s}$ . [39] provide models spanning $T_{\rm eff}\approx 30-150\,{\rm kK}$ , $\log(g)\approx 4-6$ , and $X_{\rm H,s}=0.01,0.1,0.3,0.5,0.7$ . The parameter space is not uniformly sampled, with models absent in some regions, particularly at high $T_{\rm eff}$ and low $\log(g)$ . After resampling $F_{\lambda}$ and $F_{\rm norm}$ onto a finely sampled common wavelength grid with a spacing of approximately $0.2\,{\rm\AA}$ , we linearly interpolate the spectral model grid in $T_{\rm eff}$ , $\log g$ , and $X_{\rm H,s}$ using LinearNDInterpolator from SciPy. We do not extrapolate beyond the available models. These spectral models are parameterized solely by the stellar atmospheric properties ( $T_{\rm eff}$ , $\log(g)$ , and $X_{\rm H,s}$ ) and are not associated with a particular evolutionary stage.

Synthetic photometry: we integrate the spectral flux density, $F_{\lambda}(\lambda)$ , from our interpolated grid of spectral models with the appropriate UV and optical transmission curves [99, 98, 100] to compute the synthetic flux for each bandpass. In our fitting procedure (Section IV.2.3 and IV.2.4), we scale these synthetic fluxes for a given stellar radius to obtain the observed fluxes. We then convert the flux to an apparent magnitude assuming a distance of 62.44 kpc to the SMC [38]. To account for reddening, we estimate $A_{\lambda}$ for each bandpass from $A_{V}$ using the SMC extinction curve [32], adopting $R_{V}=3.13$ . We then apply $A_{\lambda}$ to the synthetic photometry derived from the spectra to estimate the reddened magnitudes.33 3 For simplicity, we adopt the SMC extinction curve to model the total extinction toward J0040-7333. This neglects differences between the Milky Way and SMC extinction curves for the foreground dust. By integrating the [20] 3D dust map out to 2 kpc, we estimate a Milky Way foreground contribution of $A_{V}\sim 0.12$ mag.

#### IV.2.2 Spectral features

We shift the 12 MagE spectra to the stripped star’s rest frame, interpolate each spectrum onto a common wavelength grid, and coadd them into a single spectrum. We take a weighted average of the spectra, weighting each pixel by its inverse variance. We show the full coadded spectrum in Figure 4. The stacked spectrum has a signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of $\sim 45$ .

As discussed in [37] and demonstrated in the lower left panels of Figure 4, several absorption and emission features are sensitive to effective temperature. For example, the He i $\lambda 4471$ and He i $\lambda 5876$ absorption lines are only present for $T_{\rm eff}\lesssim 50\,\rm{kK}$ and $T_{\rm eff}\lesssim 60-70\,\rm{kK}$ , respectively, and N v $\lambda 4604$ absorption appears only for stripped stars with $50\,\rm{kK}\lesssim T_{\rm eff}\lesssim 90\,\rm{kK}$ .

We find that the spectrum of J0040-7333 does not show any He i $\lambda\lambda 4471,5876$ features but shows absorption in N v $\lambda 4604$ . When fitting for the stellar parameters of the stripped star, we use the presence of N v $\lambda 4604$ to construct a prior on the atmospheric parameters.

#### IV.2.3 Joint SED and spectral fits

We use the stacked MagE spectrum for spectral fitting, and use photometry from MCPS, Swift-UVOT, and UVIT for the SED fitting.44 4 We do not use photometry from SMASH because we find a systematic offset between the observed and predicted colors of MS stars. Especially in the $u-$ band, we find significant offsets which suggest calibration problems. These discrepancies may be related to color-dependent calibration systematics discussed in Nidever et al. [84]. We simultaneously fit the stacked spectra and SED and fit for four parameters: $T_{\rm eff}$ , $\log(g)$ , $X_{\rm H,s}$ , and $R$ .

We do not attempt to simultaneously fit for extinction, but instead perform the fit over a range of $A_{V}$ values. We find that given the relatively small number of data points in the SED relative to the normalized spectrum, leaving $A_{V}$ as a free parameter drives the joint fit to a solution with high $A_{V}$ that provides a poor match to the observed SED. This formally maximizes the likelihood because a higher $T_{\rm eff}$ provides a marginal improvement to the spectral fit but is unlikely to be reliable (see Appendix E for further discussion). We therefore separately estimate the reddening for J0040-7333 by comparing the observed UV and optical colors to synthetic colors of stripped stars with properties roughly matched to those of J0040-7333 ( $T_{\rm eff}=60-70\,{\rm kK}$ , $\log(g)=4.7-5.0$ , $X_{\rm H,s}=0.65$ ), reddened over the range of $A_{V}=0-1.0\,{\rm mag}$ . We find that the observed colors best match the synthetic colors for $A_{V}\approx 0.30$ mag. Because these colors lie on the Rayleigh-Jeans tail of the SED, the synthetic colors, and hence the inferred $A_{V}$ , are only weakly sensitive to the $T_{\rm eff}$ of the stripped star. To assess the systematic uncertainties associated with uncertainty in $A_{V}$ , we repeat our fit over a range of $A_{V}=0.25-0.35$ mag.

We use the following lines for our fits: He ii $\lambda 4100$ /H $\delta$ , He ii $\lambda 4200$ , He ii $\lambda 4339$ /H $\gamma$ , He i $\lambda 4471$ , He ii $\lambda 4542$ , N v $\lambda 4604$ , He ii $\lambda 4859$ /H $\beta$ , He ii $\lambda 5412$ , and He i $\lambda 5876$ . For each line, we extract a $50\,\rm{\AA}$ -wide window centered on the line and renormalize the local continuum. We then use the central $40\,\rm{\AA}$ window around the line for the fitting. We first perform a $\chi^{2}$ minimization to locate the global best-fit parameters, which we use as the initializations for the MCMC walkers. We place priors on the atmospheric parameters using the presence of the N v $\lambda 4604$ line. For each set of $T_{\rm eff}$ , $\log(g)$ , and $X_{\rm H,s}$ , we convolve the synthetic spectra to $R=4100$ and measure the equivalent width (EW) of the N v $\lambda 4604$ line. We require the synthetic spectra to show detectable absorption ( $EW\geq 0.04\,{\rm\AA}$ ) to match the observed spectral feature of J0040-7333. We reject models that do not satisfy these criteria by setting their likelihood to negative infinity. Within these bounds, we place uniform priors on all of the fit parameters. We perform the MCMC sampling with 50 walkers, using 1000 burn-in steps followed by a total of 4000 steps of sampling.

From the fit parameters ( $T_{\rm eff}$ , $\log(g)$ , $X_{\rm H,s}$ , and $R$ ), we calculate the bolometric luminosity ( $L$ ) using the Stefan-Boltzmann law: $L=4\pi\sigma_{\rm SB}R^{2}T_{\rm eff}^{4}$ . Following [37], we estimate the stripped-star mass ( $M_{\rm stripped}$ ) in two different ways. First, we estimate an evolutionary mass using a mass-luminosity relation (right panel of Figure 16) derived from the evolutionary models from [34]. The relation is derived by taking the masses and luminosities of stripped stars half-way through helium burning. Second, we compute a spectroscopic mass from the inferred surface gravity and radius.

#### IV.2.4 Joint SED and spectral fits with evolutionary tracks

We also repeat the SED and spectral fits by coupling the fit to evolutionary models of intermediate-mass stripped stars. This method allows us to constrain the stripped-star mass directly from the evolutionary tracks without relying on a mass-luminosity relation that is derived from a fixed evolutionary stage. However, it also implicitly assumes that the evolutionary tracks are correct, which introduces systematic uncertainties. Specifically, the binary-evolution assumptions adopted by [34], produce stripped stars with surface hydrogen mass fractions within a rather confined range ( $X_{\rm H,s}\approx 0.35-0.4$ ), which is lower than we infer for J0040-7333.

For these fits, we sample three free parameters: initial mass ( $M_{i}$ ), core helium mass fraction ( $X_{\rm He,c}$ ), and surface hydrogen mass fraction ( $X_{\rm H,s}$ ). For each combination of these parameters, we obtain effective temperature ( $T_{\rm eff}$ ), surface gravity ( $\log(g)$ ), bolometric luminosity ( $L$ ), radius ( $R$ ), and evolutionary mass ( $M_{\rm stripped}$ ) of the stripped star using the evolutionary models. We then use these stellar properties to generate a model SED and synthetic spectra, which we compare to the observed spectra and photometric SED. We again fix $A_{V}$ in each fit and repeat the fit for a range of $A_{V}$ .

For each run, we perform an initial fit for $M_{i}$ , $X_{\rm He,c}$ , and $X_{\rm H,s}$ using $\chi^{2}$ minimization to determine the maximum-likelihood solution, which we use to initialize the MCMC sampling. For $M_{i}$ and $X_{\rm H,s}$ , we adopt uniform priors, while for $X_{\rm He,c}$ , we adopt an evolutionary-timescale prior derived from the stellar models. We sample the evolutionary tracks uniformly in $X_{\rm He,c}$ , and assign each value of $X_{\rm He,c}$ a prior probability that is proportional to the amount of evolutionary time the model spends near that core helium fraction. For each sampled set of model parameters, we use the corresponding $T_{\rm eff}$ and $\log(g)$ to produce the synthetic spectra. Similar to the fit without evolutionary model constraints (Section IV.2.3), we require that the atmospheric parameters produce synthetic spectra with detectable N v $\lambda 4604$ absorption. We run the MCMC sampling with 50 walkers, using 1000 burn-in steps followed by a total of 4000 steps of sampling.

#### IV.2.6 Surface hydrogen mass fraction

As we demonstrate in the lower right panel of Figure 4, (see also Figure 18 in Appendix D) the surface hydrogen mass fraction is constrained by the relative strengths and the central wavelengths of blended He ii/Balmer lines, which determine the relative contributions of the hydrogen and helium to the absorption features. Visual inspection alone suggests that we can rule out a low surface hydrogen mass fraction due to the central wavelength and depth of the He ii/Balmer blended lines.

A natural question is whether the inferred high $X_{\rm{H,s}}$ could be due to Balmer absorption by an unresolved hydrogen-rich companion. If the stripped star had a surface hydrogen fraction more typical of hot stripped stars ( $X_{\rm H,s}\approx 0.3$ ), reproducing the observed strength of the He ii/Balmer blends would require a MS companion of $\sim 2\,{\rm M_{\odot}}$ . Such a companion would be too cool to exhibit He i absorption, which would otherwise make it easily identifiable in the spectrum. However, at this luminosity, it would contribute roughly half of the EWs of the Balmer lines. Such a companion would change the shape of the blended lines between epochs, including producing split line cores at maximum RV difference between the two components. However, we find that the He ii/Balmer line profiles remain stable with phase. Furthermore, because the companion would have a different RV than the stripped star, it would bias the RVs measured from blended lines. Compared to RVs derived from the pure He ii lines, we would expect systematically higher RVs near the stripped star’s RV minimum and lower RVs near its RV maximum, in both cases drawing the measured RV toward the center-of-mass RV. However, we find no evidence of such trends; see Figure 15 of Appendix B. Significant contamination by a luminous companion is therefore unlikely (and also inconsistent with the light curve; see Section IV.5), so we conclude that the measured hydrogen abundance reflects the true surface composition of the stripped star.

This inferred hydrogen abundance is unusual in the context of known hot stripped stars. Although the temperature and surface gravity inferred for J0040-7333 are consistent with the standard picture of hydrogen-poor core-helium burning stars [34, e.g., ], its surface appears to be more hydrogen rich than the previously observed population of hot and compact intermediate-mass stripped stars [37]. The inferred surface hydrogen mass fraction instead is comparable to that of partially-stripped stars [97, e.g.,], which are predicted to be cooler and more bloated [61, 19, e.g.,] compared to what we infer for J0040-7333.

Current binary evolution models predict that retaining a substantial hydrogen-rich envelope after stripping prevents a stripped star from contracting. As a result, such stars are generally not expected to reach the compact radii ( $R\sim 1\,\rm{R_{\odot}}$ ) and high effective temperatures ( $T_{\rm eff}\gtrsim 50\,{\rm{kK}}$ ) that are typical of their more fully stripped counterparts. The combination of a hot, compact structure and relatively high surface hydrogen abundance we observe for J0040-7333 is therefore difficult to reproduce with existing evolutionary models.

### IV.3 Stellar rotation

At orbital periods of $\lesssim 1\,{\rm day}$ , tides are predicted to efficiently synchronize the rotation of the helium stripped star with the binary’s orbital period [75, e.g., ]. Using the inferred orbital period and the radius of the stripped star, we can infer an equatorial rotational velocity of $2\pi R/P_{\rm orb}\approx 60\,{\rm km\,s^{-1}}$ for the stripped star for an edge-on, tidally synchronized system. In Figure 6, we show the best-fit synthetic spectra with no rotation ( $v\sin(i)=0\,\rm{km\,s^{-1}}$ ) and with tidally-synchronized rotation ( $v\sin(i)=60\,\rm{km\,s^{-1}}$ ).

We find that, at the resolution and SNR of the MagE spectra, we are unable to robustly detect rotation with $v\sin(i)=60\,{\rm km\,s^{-1}}$ . With the resolution of spectra we have, we can rule out high rotation rates and infer an upper limit of $v\sin(i)\lesssim 90\,{\rm km\,s^{-1}}$ . However, for a more robust measurement of the stellar rotation, higher-resolution data, e.g., $R\gtrsim 10,000$ , is necessary. Assuming the stripped star is tidally synchronized, measurement of $v\sin(i)$ would constrain the inclination angle of the binary and provide stronger constraints on the companion mass.

### IV.4 Constraining the companion mass

Using the orbital parameters ( $P_{\rm orb}$ , $K$ , $e$ ) and the mass of the stripped star, we estimate the mass of the companion. We calculate the binary mass function, $f_{m}$ , and numerically solve it for the companion mass, $M_{2}$ :

$$ f_{m}=\frac{M_{2}^{3}\sin^{3}i}{(M_{\rm stripped}+M_{2})^{2}}=\frac{P_{\rm orb}K^{3}}{2\pi G}(1-e^{2})^{3/2}, $$

We sample $P_{\rm orb}$ , $K$ , and $e$ from their respective MCMC posterior distributions and obtain $f_{m}=0.066\pm 0.007\,\rm{M_{\odot}}$ . We sample $M_{\rm stripped}$ from a Gaussian distribution with $\mu=3.84\,{\rm M_{\odot}}$ and $\sigma=0.54\,{\rm M_{\odot}}$ reflecting the fiducial best-fit evolutionary mass and the total uncertainty. For a given inclination angle $i$ , we numerically solve Equation 2 to obtain the corresponding companion mass. For each inclination angle, we estimate the companion mass and uncertainties using the median and the 16th/84th percentiles from the resulting companion mass distributions, respectively. We show the inferred companion mass as a function of inclination angle in Figure 7.
